notes.b: Meat is muscle, and muscle is made of fibres held together by connective tissue (the tough, stringy tissue that binds the fibres). How tough a piece of meat is depends on how much of this tissue it has and on what happens to the animal and the meat before and during cooking.
points: Age of the animal: older animals have longer, thicker muscle fibres and more connective tissue, and the collagen (the main protein of connective tissue) in it is more cross-linked, so the meat is tougher. Young animals such as veal, lamb and chicken are tender.

Activity of the muscle: muscles that work hard, such as the legs, neck, shoulder, shin and flank, have larger fibres and more connective tissue than the little-used loin, sirloin or fillet. This is why the cut of meat decides its toughness.
Treatment before slaughter: an animal that is rested and not stressed gives better meat, while poor rest or stress before slaughter lowers the quality of the meat.

Treatment after slaughter: if meat is not hung long enough, the muscle stays stiff from rigor mortis (the stiffening of muscle after death). Chilling too quickly after slaughter makes the muscle contract (cold shortening), so the meat is tough.
Cooking: high heat, fast cooking or overcooking coagulates (sets) the protein and squeezes out juices, so the meat is dry and tough.
Connective tissue and cooking: collagen is not broken down by quick dry cooking, so tough cuts need slow moist cooking.
Fat content: marbled meat (meat with fine streaks of fat through the muscle) feels juicier and more tender.
notes.tip: Examiners usually ask for two or three causes of toughness. Give the cause, then the reason: for example age or activity, then longer thicker fibres and more connective tissue.

notes.h: Methods of tenderising and their principles
notes.b: Tenderising means making tough meat softer to eat. Each method works by one of four principles: mechanical (physically breaking fibres), chemical (acid or salt), enzymic (enzymes splitting protein) or heat (slow moist cooking).
points: Hanging (maturing): after slaughter rigor mortis stiffens the muscle. During hanging in a cold room the stiffness passes, glycogen (the muscle's store of sugar) turns to lactic acid, and the meat's own proteolytic (protein-splitting) enzymes break down fibres and connective tissue. Beef is hung for about 1 to 3 weeks.
Mincing: a mincer breaks fibres and connective tissue into small pieces (a mechanical principle), so tough cuts become tender in products such as burgers and bolognese.

Pounding with a steak hammer or mallet, or cutting across the grain, breaks up the long muscle fibres and connective tissue mechanically. Piercing with needles, skewers or forks does the same and lets marinade or brine get into the meat.

Proteolytic enzymes: papain from papaya, bromelain from pineapple, ficin from figs and actinidin from kiwi split the protein bonds in muscle and collagen. They are sprinkled on or injected into the meat before cooking, and act mostly on the surface and as cooking warms the meat.

Acid marinades: lemon juice, vinegar, wine or yoghurt soften muscle protein by acid action and add flavour. A marinade works only on the surface, so it does not tenderise a whole joint or make meat safe.
Brining and curing: a salt solution dissolves some muscle proteins so the meat holds more water and stays juicy and tender during cooking, as in bacon and ham.

Slow moist cooking (stewing, braising, casseroling, pot roasting) converts collagen to gelatine, which softens the connective tissue and separates the fibres. Elastin (another connective protein) is not softened, so trim it or mince it.
Pressure cooking: steam at high pressure and temperature converts collagen to gelatine quickly, so tough cuts tenderise in much less time.
notes.tip: For each method, give the method and then its principle: say what is done and why it works. Questions have asked for one to four tenderising methods.

notes.b: Heat changes the protein, fat, colour, flavour and nutrients of meat all at once. Some changes make meat safe and tasty, and others, if the cooking goes on too long, spoil it.
points: Coagulation: heating makes the protein denature and set (coagulate), so the meat firms and its fibres harden and shrink. Overcooking makes the protein tough and dry and lowers its digestibility.
Shrinkage: water, juices and melted fat are lost as meat cooks, so it loses weight and size. Lower, slower cooking loses less.
Fat melts during cooking, and in roasting it bastes the meat as it drips. The fat that runs out can be poured away.
Collagen converts to gelatine in moist cooking, which tenderises the meat. Elastin does not change.
Myoglobin (the red pigment in muscle) denatures at cooking temperatures, so red meat changes to brown or grey and the juices turn from pink to clear in well-cooked meat.
Micro-organisms are destroyed, so thorough cooking makes meat safe to eat. Cook to 75 °C at the centre for poultry, pork, mince, sausages and burgers.

Flavour develops: extractives (flavour compounds in the meat) are released, and the Maillard reaction between amino acids and sugars at a high surface temperature browns the surface and gives a roasted flavour. Surface protein coagulates and browns.

Nutrients: correctly cooked protein stays available and is easier to digest. Water-soluble vitamins, especially thiamine (B1), and minerals dissolve into the cooking juices or drip, so use the juices in gravy or sauce. Some B vitamins are destroyed by heat, while fat-soluble vitamins are mostly retained.
notes.tip: For effects of cooking, use the vocabulary examiners look for: coagulation, firming and shrinkage, fat melts, collagen to gelatine, myoglobin colour change, Maillard flavour, loss of water-soluble vitamins and safety. Use 'coagulates' for firming and 'denatures' for the myoglobin colour change.

notes.b: Every cooking method works by moving heat into the meat in one of a few ways. Naming the way heat travels is the 'underlying principle' examiners want when you describe a method.
points: Conduction: heat passes through a solid such as a pan, so frying uses conduction through hot fat.
Convection: heat moves through a liquid or hot air, so stewing in liquid and roasting in a hot oven rely on convection.
Radiation: infrared heat travels directly from the source, so grilling and barbecuing rely on radiant heat.
Microwaves (electromagnetic waves) make the water molecules in the food vibrate, producing heat inside the food. They penetrate only about 2 to 4 cm.
Stewing: meat is simmered in a small amount of liquid at about 80 to 90 °C, which tenderises it and keeps it moist. Heat reaches the meat by conduction through the pot and convection in the liquid.
notes.tip: When you evaluate a method, always state its principle: conduction, convection or radiation.

notes.h: Suitable cooking methods for different cuts
notes.b: The best cooking method depends on how much connective tissue a cut has. Tender cuts have little, so they need only quick cooking, but tough cuts have a lot, so they need long, gentle, moist cooking to turn it to gelatine.
points: Tender cuts such as fillet, sirloin, rump steak, loin chops, lamb cutlets, pork loin and chicken breast suit dry methods: grilling, frying, roasting, stir-frying or barbecuing, which cook them quickly.
Tough cuts such as shin, chuck, brisket, neck, flank, oxtail, stewing steak and chicken legs need slow moist cooking (stewing, braising, casseroling, pot roasting, pressure cooking) or mincing.
Lamb shanks and beef shin become tender when braised slowly in liquid, because the long moist heat turns their collagen to gelatine.
Joints for roasting include leg of lamb, loin of pork, topside and whole poultry. Gammon and ham are boiled or baked, and sausages and burgers are grilled or baked.
Mince is fried and then simmered in dishes such as bolognese and chilli, or shaped into burgers and grilled. It must be cooked through.
Poultry is cooked until no pink meat remains, the juices run clear and the centre is steaming hot (75 °C at the core). It can be roasted whole or in portions, stewed or casseroled.
Liver and kidney are cooked quickly by frying or grilling, or gently braised, because long cooking toughens them, especially liver.
notes.tip: Match the method to the cut and say why: tough cuts need slow moist cooking and tender cuts need fast dry cooking. Reversing them is the most common error.

notes.b: An evaluation question asks you to judge one method of cooking meat, not list several. One well-evaluated method is better than a list.
points: An evaluation names the method, states its underlying principle (how heat reaches the food), describes its effect on the meat (texture, colour, flavour, nutrient loss, fat), and weighs advantages against disadvantages.

Stewing advantages: it tenderises tough cuts because collagen turns to gelatine, keeps the meat moist, makes use of cheap cuts, and the liquid becomes a sauce so nutrients that leached out are kept. It can be left unattended and uses little fuel, especially in a slow cooker.
Stewing disadvantages: it takes a long time, and nutrients leach into the liquid and are lost if it is discarded, giving a lower vitamin content.
Frying: it is fast and browns the surface, but it adds fat and dries or toughens the meat if overcooked.
Grilling: radiant heat browns tender cuts quickly with little added fat, because the fat drains away, but it can dry out lean meat.
Roasting: dry heat in a hot oven suits tender joints, and fat drips away from a rack.
Microwaving: it is fast and efficient, but it does not brown meat unless combined with a grill, and it can cook unevenly.
Other methods that can be evaluated include boiling, poaching, steaming, braising, pressure cooking and barbecuing. Each needs a name, a principle and an effect on the meat.
notes.tip: For a method evaluation, give the name, the principle (conduction, convection or radiation), the effects on tenderness, colour, flavour, juiciness and nutrients, and the cuts it suits. Always add at least one disadvantage.

notes.h: Low-cost meat menus for a family
notes.b: A family on a low income can still eat meat if it chooses cheaper cuts, stretches them with other foods and cooks them well. Exam menus ask for a suitable meal with reasons.
points: Choose inexpensive cuts such as mince, chicken thighs or portions, sausages, liver, shin or stewing steak, and cook them by slow moist methods such as stew, casserole, curry or shepherd's pie.
Stretch mince with vegetables or lentils; a bolognese with carrots, onions and lentils uses less meat without losing flavour.
Starchy foods such as potatoes, pasta, rice or bread complete the meal, make it filling and supply energy.
Cabbage, other vegetables, fruit and potatoes add vitamin C, which meat does not contain.
Meat supplies protein for growing children and haem iron (the well-absorbed form of iron) for teenage girls and pregnant women, so it is worth including in a low-cost family meal.
Stock made from bones, and the cooking juices, make soups and gravies that keep extractives and water-soluble vitamins in the meal.
Batch cooking a casserole and freezing the portions saves fuel and time. Slow cookers and one-pot meals also save fuel.

Give reasons for the menu: cost, nutritive value, ease of cooking, family tastes, skills and equipment, and fuel saving. Examples of two-course menus are spaghetti bolognese with an apple crumble, or vegetable soup followed by spaghetti bolognese.
notes.tip: Low-income menu questions ask for a two-course menu with meat as the main ingredient, and reasons: cost, nutrition, skills, equipment, time and taste.

keyTerms.definition: The stiffening of muscle after slaughter, during which glycogen converts to lactic acid and the meat later tenderises on hanging.
An enzyme that breaks down protein bonds in muscle and connective tissue, used to tenderise meat.
A seasoned liquid, often containing acid, in which meat is soaked to soften it and add flavour.
A concentrated salt solution used to add moisture to meat or to cure it.
Toughening of meat caused by chilling it too quickly after slaughter, which makes the muscle contract.
The setting of protein when heated, causing meat to firm and its fibres to harden.
The change in the structure of a protein caused by heat or acid, which alters its texture and colour.
The browning reaction between sugars and amino acids on the surface of meat during dry heat, which creates roasted flavours.
The transfer of heat through a solid, such as a pan or grill plate.
The transfer of heat through a liquid or air as hotter material rises and cooler material sinks.
The transfer of heat by infrared waves travelling directly from a source, such as a grill element.

questions.prompt: Describe the principle behind two methods of tenderising meat that do not rely on slow cooking.
questions.model: Mincing or pounding: physical breakdown of muscle fibres and connective tissue into smaller pieces, so the meat is softer. Proteolytic enzymes such as papain or bromelain: split protein bonds in muscle and connective tissue, softening the meat. Acid marinades: acid softens and denatures the muscle protein and adds flavour. Piercing with needles: punctures fibres and lets the marinade or brine penetrate. Each method with its principle gains the marks.

questions.prompt: Evaluate one cooking method suitable for a tough cut of meat, referring to its underlying principle, how it changes the meat, and its advantages and disadvantages for a family with limited time.
questions.model: Name the method, for example stewing. Principle: conduction and convection through a small amount of liquid at about 80 to 90 °C. Effect on the meat: collagen converts to gelatine, so the fibres soften and separate; the meat stays moist; colour changes to brown; micro-organisms are destroyed; flavour from extractives in the stock. Nutrients: water-soluble vitamins such as thiamine leach into the liquid, so the liquid is used as a sauce. Advantages: tenderises cheap tough cuts, economical, low attention needed while cooking, can cook a whole meal in one pot. Disadvantages: long cooking time and fuel use, so less suitable where time is short; loss of nutrients if the liquid is discarded. Conclusion weighs these against the family's needs, for example batch cooking and freezing portions to save time.
